title: Missiles Instead of Drones: Iran Starts Hitting Tanker Engine Rooms as OPEC+ Meets a Market It Can No Longer Move
subhead: At least 23 ship attacks were logged around Hormuz in the first two weeks of October, with five hitting engine rooms — and Iran is now using infrared-guided missiles rather than drones. Meanwhile OPEC+ left November quotas unchanged, the UAE is producing at near-record levels after its exit, and Japan is months from running out of yttrium.

sections.heading: Hormuz: Iran Is Now Disabling Ships, Not Just Frightening Them
sections.body:
The character of the Persian Gulf attacks has changed. At least 23 incidents involving ships attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz were logged in the first two weeks of October, with at least five reporting impacts to their engine rooms, according to naval groups in the region and security-consultant alerts compiled by Bloomberg and reported by gCaptain. There were no engine-damage attacks at all in September.

Two things are driving it. Iran has begun using more missiles rather than drones, shipping and maritime security officials told Bloomberg; infrared-guided missiles home in on the hottest part of a ship — the engine room — and carry larger payloads. 'What we're seeing is an increase in the frequency of attacks, and therefore, more damage in engine rooms and disabling fire,' said Phillip Belcher, marine director at Intertanko. Jakob Larsen of Bimco noted the choice is deliberate: hitting engines or the bridge 'maximizes damage while keeping the risk of an oil spill relatively low.'

The operational effect is what matters. A vessel with a destroyed engine room is out of service for months, not days. At least two recently hit vessels sank last week, including a container ship struck in Hormuz — after which Pakistan's Hydrographic Services warned of containers adrift near the UAE. 'In a region where few owners are willing to put ships in, every VLCC hit is material,' analysts at Oil Brokerage Ltd. wrote on 19 October.

Flows are still moving. Kpler preliminary data put the seven-day average of Middle East oil exports fractionally above pre-war levels, and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said shipments are running at about 80% of normal. Iraq said Monday its exports are approaching pre-war levels. But the binding constraint is no longer barrels in the ground — it is ships available to carry them.
sections.whyItMatters: The war's choke point has migrated from geology to shipping capacity. Even if a peace deal lands tomorrow, a tanker fleet with months-long repair queues cannot be conjured back, which is why analysts now expect the supply shock to outlast the conflict itself.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Holds Quotas Steady Into a Market It Cannot Reach
sections.body:
OPEC+ agreed to keep November oil output targets unchanged, per EnergyNow. The decision is close to irrelevant in practice: with Hormuz constrained and Gulf producers selling spot cargoes instead of honoring term volumes, a quota adjustment changes little that a buyer can actually lift.

The bloc's internal politics are the more consequential story. The UAE has left OPEC and is now producing at near-record levels, according to sources cited by EnergyNow — a direct challenge to Riyadh's ability to set the group's ceiling. Reuters columnist Ron Bousso argued in a column carried by EnergyNow that the UAE exit strips OPEC of clout and risks a bitter price war, and separately that OPEC is likely the loser in the Gulf's post-war race for market share.

Concrete evidence of that shift is showing up in term contracts. Asian refiners and Saudi Arabia are locked in a dispute over 2027 term supply: refiners want this year's spot purchases counted toward their 2026 contractual volumes, since sellers could not deliver the term cargoes, while Riyadh insists buyers commit to higher volumes in 2027 because they missed this year's obligations, Bloomberg reported via Oilprice.com. The dispute has already slowed Asian purchases of November-loading Saudi crude. Abu Dhabi's ADNOC, by contrast, has allowed some Asian refiners to count spot supply toward term volumes.
sections.whyItMatters: A producer cartel that cannot deliver its own contracted barrels loses the ability to discipline buyers — and Riyadh is discovering that its leverage now sits in contract law rather than in production policy. The 2027 term talks will set the price architecture for the post-war market.

sections.heading: The Real Bottleneck Is Freight, and It Is Rewriting Trade Routes
sections.body:
Tanker rates have hit records, and buyers are re-engineering supply chains around them. Asian refiners are shifting to smaller tankers and long-term charters, and buying crude on a delivered basis rather than free-on-board, refining and trading sources told Reuters. The mechanism: rising Hormuz volumes are largely ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, which tie up supertankers for weeks waiting outside the strait and starve other routes of VLCCs.

The price map has inverted. Dated Brent traded at a record $20 per barrel premium to Brent last week; Norway's Johan Sverdrup hit a record $24 premium to Brent, per Wood Mackenzie. West African grades have slumped to record-low discounts, some at minus $20 a barrel, to offset freight. The US Gulf Coast-to-Asia arbitrage is effectively shut.

Banks are now building the bypass thesis into their outlook. HSBC chief executive Georges Elhedery, speaking at the HSBC Future Forum in Dubai, said alternative routes could make Hormuz 'redundant' within five years, per Reuters. The evidence base: Saudi Arabia plans to raise its East-West pipeline to 10 million bpd from 7 million within two to three years, per Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman; Kuwait is hunting storage outside the region; Iraq is weighing a revived pipeline to Syria's Mediterranean coast.
sections.whyItMatters: Freight, not crude, is now the marginal cost that determines where barrels go. That is a durable change — pipeline and storage capacity built on this logic will outlast the war and permanently reduce what Hormuz can extract from importers.

sections.heading: Asia Is Paying for the Gulf Crisis in Rare Earths, Not Just Barrels
sections.body:
Away from the Gulf, China's export controls are producing a measurable industrial emergency in Japan. Tokyo could run short of yttrium — a heat-resistant rare earth used in jet engines, turbines, cars and semiconductor plasma-etching chambers — as early as the end of this year, the Financial Times reported. A Japanese official put the timeline at 'months, not years.'

The price gap is the clearest measure of the squeeze: yttrium oxide costs about $9 a kilogram inside China and $1,150 outside, per Argus — a 179-fold spread in two years. Japan's imports of yttrium oxide fell 74% in the first half of 2026 versus two years earlier, and Chinese customs data showed shipments of yttrium, dysprosium and terbium to Japan at zero in June. Japan has been drawing down stockpiles to keep factories running, and has asked Washington to press Beijing for relief.

The trigger is political: Beijing tightened exports after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said a Taiwan conflict could pose an existential threat to Japan. A senior US official said China is letting Japan buy only 'the bare minimum it needs' while meeting about two-thirds of its commitments to America. The lesson for Europe is uncomfortable — after the 2010 embargo Japan spent fifteen years cutting dependence from roughly 90% to 60%, but for heavy rare earths it remains near 100% dependent.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is the best-prepared buyer in the world on rare earths, and it is still months from a shortage. That result argues against stockpiling and diversification as sufficient answers, and it puts a hard clock on Europe's new heavy-rare-earth capacity — Caremag's Lacq plant, due to start at the end of this year at up to 600 tonnes a year, about 15% of global output.

sections.heading: Russia: Production Slips for a Tenth Month as Ukraine Picks Its Targets
sections.body:
Russian seaborne crude exports averaged 3.59 million bpd in the four weeks to 18 October, down 110,000 bpd, per Bloomberg tanker tracking cited by Oilprice.com. Weekly shipments fell 390,000 bpd to 3.13 million bpd, the lowest since March, after the Baltic port of Primorsk stopped loading for about three days. Weekly export value dropped roughly $380 million to $2.33 billion, a six-week low.

Underlying production is worse than the export wobble. OPEC secondary-source estimates put September Russian output at 8.64 million bpd — the lowest since mid-2020 and the tenth consecutive monthly decline. Ukrainian drone strikes keep hitting refining: an attack on the Ryazan refinery last Thursday knocked out one of four primary processing units.

Moscow is responding on two fronts. It restricted public disclosure of refinery output, export contracts, shipping routes and tanker coordinates under a 28 September decree. And it has opened a new export vector: commercial shipments from Rosneft's Vostok Arctic project began in September, about 250,000 tonnes on three ice-class tankers, expected to average 150,000 bpd this year against an original 2 million bpd ambition.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia's capacity to absorb the diesel waiver Washington granted last week is shrinking — ten straight months of declining output means sanctions relief buys less supply than the market assumed. Vostok Arctic at 7.5% of its designed throughput also shows the Arctic route is not the answer Moscow has been selling.

sections.heading: Norway's September Gas Drop Lands at the Worst Possible Moment
sections.body:
Norway's natural gas output fell 12.6% in September to 298.4 million cubic metres per day from 341.6 mcm/d in August, preliminary figures from the Norwegian Offshore Directorate show. Total petroleum production averaged about 3.77 million boepd, down 10.4% month-on-month and 4% below forecast. Oil fell 145,000 bpd, or 7.7%, to 1.73 million bpd.

Most of it is scheduled: Gassco had warned that maintenance could cut Norwegian export capacity by about 20%, roughly 71 mcm/d, before the end of September. Gas output also came in 6.7% under NOD's forecast, and the figures do not establish how much was maintenance versus operational trouble. A separate drag persists: Shell's Ormen Lange field is expected to deliver about 7.9 mcm/d less until 1 February 2027.

Context matters for the reading: Norwegian gas production was still 5.1% above September 2025, and first-nine-month petroleum output is 2.9% higher year-on-year. Oil output beat the monthly forecast by 0.7%.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's largest pipeline supplier is entering winter with a monthly slump and a known multi-month field outage, on top of storage that sat around 74% in mid-October. It raises the cost of any cold snap — but the year-on-year numbers say this is maintenance timing, not a supply failure.

bottomLine: Iran's switch to infrared-guided missiles aimed at engine rooms is the day's most consequential development: it attacks the tanker fleet itself rather than the cargo, and a fleet takes far longer to rebuild than a peace deal takes to sign. OPEC+ holding November quotas steady was the quiet admission that the group's decisions no longer bind — the binding constraints are freight, repair queues and term-contract disputes with Asian refiners. And the day's other energy shock is in rare earths, where Japan — the world's most experienced hedger — is months from running out of yttrium at a 179-fold price spread to China. Two different chokepoints, one shared lesson: this quarter, control over logistics and processing beats control over reserves.
sources: Bloomberg via gCaptain, Reuters, Oilprice.com, EnergyNow, Financial Times, European Business Magazine, Argus, Wood Mackenzie, Kpler, Norwegian Offshore Directorate (NOD), Gassco, Intertanko, Bimco, Oil Brokerage Ltd., HSBC, OPEC secondary-source estimates
